analysis.one_liner: Requires the Interior Department to auction off the most oil-rich public offshore waters to drillers.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 243-179 on May 12, 2011, with 222 of 239 voting Republicans in favor, but the Senate never voted and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the offshore leasing law to force the Interior Department to offer for drilling at least half the unleased acreage in the offshore areas with the biggest oil and gas deposits, plus any offshore area a state governor asks to open. It also would have required leasing in any offshore planning area estimated to hold more than 2.5 billion barrels of oil or 7.5 trillion cubic feet of gas, and set a national goal of adding 3 million barrels of oil per day by 2027. In practice, it would have taken the pace and location of offshore drilling decisions away from Interior Department review and locked them into law. The House passed it, the Senate never acted, and it expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain guaranteed access to lease sales in the most resource-rich federal offshore waters, on a congressionally mandated schedule, without waiting for the Interior Department's own planning process. Governors who want drilling off their coasts could trigger lease sales on request.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to require the Interior Secretary to offer for leasing at least 50% of available unleased acreage in each offshore planning area with the largest recoverable oil and gas resources, with emphasis on the most geologically promising acreage [S5].
It requires lease offerings in any planning area estimated to contain more than 2.5 billion barrels of oil or 7.5 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, using a fixed 2006 resource assessment [S5].
It requires any state subdivision of a planning area to be offered for leasing if that state's governor requests it [S5].

It sets a mandatory domestic production goal for the 2012-2017 leasing program: at least 3 million more barrels of oil and 10 billion more cubic feet of natural gas per day by 2027, aimed at domestic demand and reduced foreign dependence [S5].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the costs: it gives up control over when and where public offshore waters are opened to drilling, since the mandated lease sales would override the Interior Department's own planning. Coastal communities face the increased risk that comes with expanded offshore drilling, and nothing in the bill requires the oil produced to be sold in the United States — an amendment to that effect was rejected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities and the general public

drawbacks.text: The bill converts offshore leasing decisions from an agency planning process into statutory mandates, removing the Interior Department's discretion to weigh environmental and coastal impacts before opening specific waters [S5].

An amendment offered by Rep. Holt that would have required all oil and gas produced under the bill's leasing programs to be sold in the United States rather than exported, and cut nonproducing leases in half by 2017, failed 180-243, so the bill's domestic-supply rationale was not matched by a domestic-sales guarantee [S7][S8].

Every amendment offered on the floor to modify or condition the drilling expansion — including ones from Reps. Connolly, Markey, Keating, Tsongas, Brown, Thompson, and Inslee — was rejected during House consideration [S7].

Requiring lease sales in the most resource-rich offshore areas necessarily expands offshore drilling activity, which carries spill risk to coastal environments and to fishing and tourism economies that depend on clean water.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose — more domestic oil and gas and less dependence on foreign energy — was real, and more drilling can add supply over time. But the design took the decision-making away from public planning and locked in lease sales by formula, and the House rejected the one amendment that would have guaranteed the added oil stayed in the domestic market. The design favored drilling companies' access to public resources more than it reliably delivered consumer benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on May 12, 2011, was placed on the Senate calendar two days later, and never came up for a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported on a 29-14 vote on April 13, 2011, and reported it amended on May 2 [S7].
The House passed the bill 243-179 on May 12, 2011; 222 of 239 voting Republicans supported it and 170 of 192 voting Democrats opposed it [S8].
Before the final vote, the House rejected 180-243 a motion to recommit that would have required the oil to be sold domestically rather than exported [S7][S8].
The Senate received the bill on May 16, 2011, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Calendar under General Orders, where it remained without a vote [S7][S5].
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities and the public kept the existing system, in which the Interior Department decides when and where offshore waters are leased. Oil and gas companies gained nothing from the bill's death, but lost nothing either, since offshore drilling continued under the existing program.

for.name: Doc Hastings
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Natural Resources
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, moved it through subcommittee and a 29-14 committee markup in six weeks, and reported it to the House [S1][S7].

for.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
for.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing, then marked up and ordered the bill reported amended by a 29-14 vote [S7].

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor after it was placed on the calendar; it died there.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed the bill and threatened a veto; the bill's title was framed as reversing his post-spill offshore drilling policies.

against.name: Rush Holt
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit with instructions requiring all oil and gas produced under the bill's leases to be sold in the U.S. and cutting nonproducing leases 50% by 2017; rejected 180-243 [S7][S8].

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party: 222 of 239 voting Republicans backed the bill while 170 of 192 voting Democrats opposed it, and the pre-floor motion to recommit failed on a nearly identical party split [S8].

industries.note: The bill would have compelled the Interior Department to auction the most resource-rich unleased federal offshore acreage on a fixed schedule and open any area a governor requests, giving drillers guaranteed access to public waters without agency discretion. The House rejected an amendment to require the resulting oil to be sold domestically [S5][S8].

Mandated lease sales in the most prospective offshore areas would have expanded drilling activity off more coastlines, and drilling in those waters carries spill risk to the fisheries and beaches these industries depend on [S5].
